newsitem.title: UK: European debt futures slide on robust US jobs data.
newsitem.headline: European debt futures slide on robust US jobs data.

text.p: European debt markets sank late on Friday after the U.S. reported much stronger jobs growth in December than markets expected.

Although the data included the strong Christmas selling period and covered a longer period than usual, analysts said the numbers pointed to continuing strength in the U.S. economy and a possible interest rate rise ahead.
"It obviously shows the U.S economy does have strength," said Mark Bays, a trader on the LIFFE floor in London. "The biggest sell-off is going to be in the States."
At 1352 GMT, March German Bund futures were quoted at 100.15, off their lows at 99.93 but below the 100.37 level quoted before the data.

Gilt futures managed to stay in positive terroritory at 108-31, but were well below the 109-11 posted pre-payrolls. French bond futures also slithered lower while Italian BTPs lunged down then regained some losses.
Meanwhile, March T-bond futures on the CBOT suffered a heavy blow, falling as low as 109-29 before nipping back to 110-06, down 1-7/32 on the day.
The data showed U.S. payrolls grew by 262,000 in December.
Economists were expecting a rise of around 192,000. November's figure was also revised up to 127,000 from 118,000.
Analysts said the six cent rise in average hourly earnings to $12.05 could prove inflationary.
"The data was decidedly negative," said Tom Hobson, director of technical analysis at Merrill Lynch in London. "Many people will interpret it as wage inflation surfacing."
Analysts were divided over whether European bonds, which were cautiously building a base after tripping down in early January, could withstand a major Treasuries rout.
The T-note/Bund 10-year yield spread was quoted at 83 basis points, well in Bunds' favour compared with 73 before the data.
"I do believe the U.S. activity is negative for European bond markets," said Hobson. "It will completely take away their constuctive tone now."
But Bays at Mees Pierson expected European bonds to outperform, against a background of much slower economic growth.
Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Co-operative Bank in London, said he would look to buy the market on dips, although they may have to correct a bit further.

"Gilts still have very strong support at 108-00," he said. "We are three-quarters of a point away from that but come Monday or Tuesday as we move towards there, you should see some buying coming back into market."
On Bunds, he added, "If we get down to 99.80 in the Bunds, that is where the market should get a little bit of a bounce."
